name: Yara Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a corporate lawyer at Pryce Hollander, a regional firm of about forty lawyers, and I advise family-owned businesses: farms, haulage firms, a chain of three garden centres. A normal day is shareholder agreements, a call about who takes over when the founder retires, and sometimes sitting between a father and son who haven't spoken in a month. I like keeping families and businesses together. What wears me out is the Companies House forms, and the evenings when a family row lands in my inbox at ten at night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools for any of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Now and then, for first drafts of board minutes and standard share transfer forms, since the senior associates started using it last year and nothing went wrong. I'd never use it for a succession plan; those are about people. I'm twenty-seven, engaged to Luca, who runs his family's bakery with his father, and I've got about nine months saved plus a share in my parents' rental flat. We go to Mass on Sundays, and his mother still hasn't forgiven me for being late to the engagement lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That suits me. Most of my clients would say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good tools help, but family businesses run on trust and a handshake, and that doesn't change. My farmers and hauliers would nod along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my career goes as planned. Senior associate in two years, maybe partner by thirty-five, and Pryce Hollander keeps its family business clients because nobody else in the county does it as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tool for minutes and forms, a bit more as it improves. Luca and I would marry next autumn and keep saving, about £800 a month from me. I'd keep up my evening course in family business mediation, which I'm halfway through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family businesses run on trust. Has that ever gone wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, when a brother signed a deal without telling his sister, and the business nearly split. That's why I still sit in the room. A father and son who haven't spoken for a month won't sign a succession plan written by a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the wedding look like in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The parish church, then the reception in the bakery yard, with Luca's father baking the cake himself. He's already arguing about the size of it. In this world, nothing gets in the way of that.

say: Family businesses run on **trust and a handshake**.
Good tools help, but **people** still decide who takes over the farm.
think: My career goes **as planned**: senior associate in two years.
Pryce Hollander keeps its **family business** clients, since nobody else in the county does it as well.
do: Use the AI tool **a bit more** for minutes and forms.
Save about **£800 a month** toward married life with Luca.
S0.quote: A father and son who haven't spoken for a month won't sign a succession plan written by a computer.
fieldNote: She's **secure**: strong clients, savings and a share in a rental flat.
Her work is **relational**, which she sees as shielded.
She **adopts tools** only after seniors prove them, true to her steady nature.

steps.text: Keep advising farms and haulage firms on succession at Pryce Hollander
Save £800 a month toward married life with Luca
Marry Luca next autumn with the reception in the bakery yard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's more real. The forms and the drafting are exactly what it would take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms should use AI for paperwork and keep people for decisions. I'd also say small businesses need simpler rules, not more, so they can adapt without paying lawyers for every change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, half my billable hours are drafting and forms, so the firm would need fewer associates like me. My edge is the families who ask for me by name. I think I'm safe for a few years, but the trainees aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tool every day once the seniors do, maybe from next spring. I'd finish the mediation course and ask to lead family meetings, which no software will run. And I'd help Luca's father buy the new oven he's been putting off, since their bakery is the safer half of our household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not frightened, but I'd keep checking which way the wind blows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help with an oven. How much, and why now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About £8,000 from my savings. My fiancé Luca's family bakery is the safer half of our household now, which is not what anyone expected when a lawyer got engaged to a baker. Bread still needs hands at four in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two trainees who started in September. They're both bright, and I'd tell them to learn the families, not just the forms, because the forms are going.

say: Use AI for **paperwork**, keep people for **decisions**.
Small businesses need **simpler rules** so they can adapt cheaply.
think: Half my hours are **drafting and forms**, so fewer associates are needed.
Families asking for me **by name** keep me safe for a few years.
do: Use the AI tool **every day** from next spring.
Finish the **mediation course** and lead family meetings.
Lend **£8,000** toward the bakery's new oven.
feel: **Uneasy**, watching which way the wind blows.
S1.quote: My fiancé Luca's family bakery is the safer half of our household now, which is not what anyone expected when a lawyer got engaged to a baker.
fieldNote: She sees her **relational work** as the part that survives.
She **invests** in the hands-on household business as a hedge.
She'd adopt AI daily only **after seniors** do, consistent with her steady pace.

steps.text: Use the firm's drafting tool daily from next spring
Finish the family business mediation course and lead family meetings
Lend £8,000 toward a new oven for Luca's family bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's before the wedding photos are even framed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say families and communities would have to hold together, and that people should look to their own before the government. I'd also say firms owe their staff an honest warning, not a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as it is goes by 2029. Drafting, advice, even the succession plans, a machine that thinks as well as a person can do them cheaper. The robots coming three years later doesn't help me at the desk, but it gives Luca's bakery till 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first six months I'd move into the bakery's business side: the books, the contracts, the expansion to a second shop. I'd cut spending, no honeymoon abroad, and keep my savings and the flat share untouched. We'd bring the wedding forward to spring, small, just family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd expect to lose my job, and I'd be asking Our Lady for patience every night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bakery gets till 2031. What happens after that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's a different question. Robots can probably knead dough by 2031, but people will still queue at a bakery where the owner knows their name. That's my hope, anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring the wedding forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'd want us settled before everything shifts. Family is the one thing a machine can't replace, so I'd want ours properly started.

say: Families and communities must **hold together**; look to your own first.
Firms owe staff an **honest warning**, not a surprise.
think: My **job as it is** goes by 2029.
The robot delay gives the **bakery until 2031**, not me.
do: Move into the **bakery's business side** within six months.
Cut the **honeymoon abroad** and keep savings untouched.
Bring the **wedding forward** to spring, just family.
feel: **Alarmed**, expecting to lose her job and praying for patience.
S2.quote: Robots can probably knead dough by 2031, but people will still queue at a bakery where the owner knows their name.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job**, so the mood is alarmed.
The household hedge is the **bakery**, given three more years by the robot delay.
Her faith and **family-first** outlook shape both her worry and her plan.

steps.text: Run the bakery's books, contracts and second-shop plans
Drop the honeymoon abroad and other big spending
Bring the wedding forward to a small spring service
Keep her savings and the flat share untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Thirty-two. That's time to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and families should use it. I'd tell the farmers I advise to plan their succession now, while there are still lawyers like me to help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the firm job lasts three or four years. In that time, I'd help Luca's bakery grow into two or three shops, so we've got a family business of our own when my job fades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Pryce Hollander and use the AI tools more as they improve. I'd put about £20,000 into opening the bakery's second shop in year two. We'd marry next autumn as planned and think about children a bit later, maybe at thirty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I'd be busy, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd tell farmers to plan succession now. Is that partly for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. I'd be busy for a few years, and that's good for the firm and for me. Mostly it's honest advice; a family that plans early fights less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does putting £20,000 into the bakery mean if it fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would hurt. But I'd rather lose money on a bakery we built than keep it in a bank waiting for the axe to fall.

say: Five years is a **fair warning**, and families should use it.
Farmers should plan **succession now**, while lawyers can still help.
think: The firm job lasts **three or four years**.
Growing the bakery to **two or three shops** gives us our own business.
do: Stay at the firm and use **AI tools** more as they improve.
Put about **£20,000** into the bakery's second shop in year two.
Marry next autumn and wait on **children** till about thirty.
S3.quote: I'd rather lose money on a bakery we built than keep it in a bank waiting for the axe to fall.
fieldNote: Five years gives her **control**, so the mood eases to anxious.
She **invests** in the family bakery rather than retraining.
She shifts **children** a little later, a quiet cost of the timeline.

steps.text: Put about £20,000 into the bakery's second shop in year two
Use the firm's improving AI tools on drafting and forms
Marry next autumn and plan children around thirty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Thirty-seven. I'd hope to have two children by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty for families who work hard and plan, and I'd say it at the parish council. Apprenticeships for young people, not more debt for degrees that won't hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could have a proper career first: senior associate, perhaps partner. Then step back into the bakery and family as the machines come. I'd have the money and the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for partner by thirty-four and save hard. I'd help the bakery grow slowly, one new shop every few years. I'd use the AI tools as the firm adopts them, no faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's there, but with ten years I'd feel I could steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said apprenticeships, not degrees. Would you have done law in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but I'd have done an apprenticeship at a firm instead of three years of debt. With ten years' warning I'd build a law career first and then step back into the bakery, which is more than most lawyers will get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger brother Rui. He's nineteen and starting an accounting degree. I'd want him to get a trade alongside it, maybe at the bakery, because accounting is the very first thing these machines will do.

say: Ten years is **plenty** for families who work hard and plan.
Young people need **apprenticeships**, not more debt for degrees.
think: I could have a **proper career** first, perhaps partner.
Then step back into the **bakery and family** as machines arrive.
do: Aim for **partner** by thirty-four and save hard.
Grow the bakery slowly, **one shop** every few years.
Use **AI tools** as the firm adopts them, no faster.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning I'd build a law career first and then step back into the bakery, which is more than most lawyers will get.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her **keep her career** and still have a fallback.
Her worry moves to her **younger brother's** accounting degree.
Her **traditional** views show in favouring apprenticeships over degrees.

steps.text: Aim for partner by thirty-four and save hard
Help the bakery open one new shop every few years
Adopt AI tools as Pryce Hollander rolls them out

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my job would go just as Luca and I were starting a family. What would help is firms giving staff an honest warning and time, and simpler rules for small family businesses, so a bakery can grow without drowning in forms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what keeps people steady. For me it's Mass on Sunday and Luca's family at the table. Machines can take the work, but they can't sit at our family table on a Sunday.

headlineQuote: Machines can take the work, but they can't sit at our family table on a Sunday.
portrait: A 27-year-old **corporate lawyer** advising family-owned farms, haulage firms and garden centres.
She's engaged to Luca, who runs his **family bakery**, with nine months saved and a flat share.
She uses AI **now and then**, after senior colleagues proved it, never for succession plans.
Calm in AI Plateau, she becomes **alarmed** at AGI by 2028 and moves into the bakery business.
She leans on **faith and family**, and wants apprenticeships and simpler rules for small firms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job would go just as she starts a family.
whatWouldHelp: Firms giving staff an **honest warning** and time to adjust.
**Simpler rules** so small family businesses can grow without drowning in forms.
